from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        lecture_lines = [
            "Distributions model how data outcomes are spread.",
            "A uniform distribution shows all outcomes are equal.",
            "Most real-world data is not uniform or simple."

        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution", lecture_lines)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF9900"))
        # Animate dot spread
        self.play(*[
            dot.animate.move_to(self.grid[f"{chr(ord('B') + (i%4))}{1 + (i%6)}"])
            for i, dot in enumerate(dots)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00CCFF"))
        mean_dot = Dot(color="#00CCFF", radius=0.2)
        self.place_at_grid(mean_dot, 'D3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(mean_dot))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Power of Sample Size (n)", [
            "Sample size, n, is our magic number.",
            "Small samples reveal the original messy distribution.",
            "Larger samples narrow the spread of means."
        ])

        # Prepare base objects
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-4, 4, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        
        # We need to render the curves. Using standard normal as approximation for demonstration.
        # Line 1: n=1 (Wide)
        curve1 = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-(x**2)/2) / np.sqrt(2*np.pi), color="#FF0000")
        # Line 2: n=5 (Narrower)
        curve2 = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-(x**2)/(2*0.5)) / np.sqrt(2*np.pi*0.5), color="#FF00FF")
        # Line 3: n=100 (Peak)
        curve3 = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-(x**2)/(2*0.05)) / np.sqrt(2*np.pi*0.05), color="#00FFFF")

        group = VGroup(axes, curve1)
        self.place_in_area(group, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.6)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FF0000")
        self.play(Create(group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")
        curve2.match_style(curve1)
        self.play(Transform(curve1, curve2))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        curve3.match_style(curve1)
        self.play(Transform(curve1, curve3))
        
        label = Text("n=100", font_size=20, color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(label, "C5")
        self.play(Write(label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application: Why This Matters", [
            "CLT lets us estimate population parameters accurately.",
            "It enables reliable hypothesis testing and confidence intervals.",
            "Engineers use it to infer quality from samples."
        ])
        
        # --- Create Visuals ---
        # 1. Chaotic stock data (erratic lines)
        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 10, 1], y_range=[-2, 2, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        data = FunctionGraph(lambda x: np.sin(x**2) + np.random.normal(0, 0.2), color="#FF3333")
        chart = VGroup(axes, data)
        self.place_in_area(chart, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        # 2. Bell Curve for CLT
        bell = FunctionGraph(lambda x: 1.5 * np.exp(-x**2), x_range=[-2, 2], color="#33FF33")
        self.place_in_area(bell, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.6)
        bell.set_opacity(0)
        
        # 3. Arrow
        arrow = Arrow(start=self.grid["F4"], end=self.grid["D4"], color=WHITE)
        arrow.set_opacity(0)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(chart))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FF3333")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(bell))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#33FF33")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(arrow))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary & Key Takeaways", [
            "CLT works for any underlying population distribution.",
            "It specifically describes the distribution of sample averages.",
            "Large samples yield highly predictable, tight bell curves."
        ])
        
        # Elements to animate
        takeaway_1 = Text("CLT: Any Distribution", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        takeaway_2 = Text("Distribution of Averages", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        takeaway_3 = Text("Large Samples = Bell Curves", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        
        group = VGroup(takeaway_1, takeaway_2, takeaway_3).arrange(DOWN, buff=0.5)
        self.place_in_area(group, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Arrows
        arrow1 = Arrow(takeaway_1.get_bottom(), takeaway_2.get_top(), color="#AAAAAA")
        arrow2 = Arrow(takeaway_2.get_bottom(), takeaway_3.get_top(), color="#AAAAAA")
        arrows = VGroup(arrow1, arrow2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(takeaway_1))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(takeaway_2), Create(arrow1))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFD700")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(takeaway_3), Create(arrow2))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFD700")
        
        # Final fade to dot
        final_dot = Dot(color="#00CCFF", radius=0.2)
        final_dot.move_to(group.get_center())
        
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(
            FadeOut(self.lecture),
            FadeOut(self.title),
            FadeOut(group),
            FadeOut(arrows),
            FadeIn(final_dot)
        )
        self.play(final_dot.animate.scale(5), run_time=2)
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): The Magic of Averages

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution
sections.content: Briefly define a probability distribution. Introduce the 'Uniform Distribution' (where everything is equally likely) and show a flat histogram vs. a 'Normal Distribution' (bell curve). Explain that real-world data is often messy and non-normal.
sections.example: Visualizing a dice roll: A single die has a uniform distribution (flat). If you roll it, you are as likely to get a 1 as a 6.

sections.title: The CLT Paradox: From Chaos to Order
sections.content: Introduce the core theorem: Regardless of the shape of the initial population, the distribution of the *sample means* will approach a normal distribution as the sample size increases. Use animations to show 'chaos' collapsing into a bell curve.
sections.example: Imagine 1,000 Shiba Inus with wildly different weights. If you pick one dog, you don't know the result. But if you pick 30 dogs, weigh them, and average them—and repeat this process—the averages will form a perfect bell curve.

sections.title: The Power of Sample Size (n)
sections.content: Explain that 'n' is the magic number. Visualize n=1 (the original messy shape) vs. n=5 vs. n=30. As n grows, the spread (standard error) narrows, and the bell curve becomes more pronounced.
sections.example: An online game character's loot drop rate is random. If you kill 1 enemy, you get 'random' loot. If you kill 30 enemies and take the average value of loot, your results will become highly predictable.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Why This Matters
sections.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'bridge' in statistics. It allows us to perform hypothesis testing and build confidence intervals even when we don't know the original population distribution.
sections.example: A quality control engineer in a smartphone factory doesn't need to test every single phone. By taking small batches (samples), the CLT allows them to estimate the average battery life of the entire million-unit production run.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaways
sections.content: Recap: 1. CLT works for ANY distribution. 2. It's about the distribution of AVERAGES. 3. Larger sample sizes yield tighter, more accurate bell curves.
sections.example: Final visual: A screen split showing 'Raw Data' (jagged/messy) transforming into a 'Sampling Distribution' (smooth bell curve) as the sample size slider moves from 1 to 100.
